newsitem.title: USA: Heating oil prices rise as temperatures seen dropping.
newsitem.headline: Heating oil prices rise as temperatures seen dropping.

text.p: Heating oil prices rallied in New York Tuesday as demand was seen increasing on forecasts of subnormal temperatures in the U.S. Northeast and Midwest at a time when inventories are low.
"We may be seeing concerned buying by consumers who feel they need to load up in case there is a shortage," said A.G. Edwards analyst Bill O'Grady.
Stronger oil prices contributed to a rise of 1.03 points to 245.50 points in the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 futures contracts.
Gold was, however, among the day's losers as further news emerged on a proposed sale by the International Monetary Fund.
Heating oil for December delivery finished 1.83 cents higher at 73.68 cents a gallon on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Heating oil's rally paced gains in the rest of the oil complex, with December crude ending up 61 cents at $24.49 a barrel, and December gasoline settling 1.62 cents higher at 67.39 cents a gallon.

"It's definitely the cold weather behind this," said Rita Beale, analyst with Fimat USA Futures in Houston. Beale said cold weather on both sides of the Atlantic spurred gains in heating oil, as it received its initial boost from higher gas oil futures on London's International Petroleum Exchange.
December gas oil, the European equivalent of heating oil, ended $3.00 a metric ton higher at $221.50 on reports of snow in Europe.

Meanwhile, the National Weather Service's six-to-10-day forecast called for temperatures to be below normal in the Northeast and Midwest. Weather Services Corp. forecast temperatures as much as 8 degrees below normal this week and lower still into the weekend.
Gold prices on New York's Commodity Exchange (COMEX) fell as further news emerged on a proposed sale of 5 million ounces by the IMF to finance debt relief for 20 of the world's poorest nations.
"Gold came under extra pressure late in the day on more news about the IMF gold sale," said Credit Lyonnais Rouse's New York chief bullion dealer, Scott Mehlman.

IMF treasurer David Williams told a London conference that, if the proposed IMF gold sale of 5 million ounces goes ahead, about 500,000 ounces would be sold at a time, amounting to about 7 percent of daily market turnover.
The sale was first mooted at a meeting of G7 finance ministers last year.
Market sentiment had already turned bearish late last week after heavy selling by gold producers stalled a brisk rally and turned prices lower.
A slowdown in demand from the jewelry sector also contributed to the market's weakness.
"There are more bears about now," one London gold dealer. "This time of year you get selloffs because the jewelry industry has done its business and business is very quiet."
December gold closed down $1.30 an ounce at $378.40.
